text: One in 500 people has this disease. A test catches 99% of cases and wrongly flags 1% of the healthy. If yours says positive, what's the chance you're sick? Pick a number. Most doctors and medical students, given a problem like this, got it wrong. Their most common answer was the test's own accuracy, here 99%. You'd start treatment today. Check that rule by counting. Here are 10,000 people, and suppose half of them are sick. Test everyone. 99% of the sick light up, and 1% of the healthy. Of the 5,000 who lit up, 99% are sick. Here, the rule holds. Now make the disease rare, like yours, one in 500. That leaves 20 sick people. Run the same test. About 20 sick people light up, plus 1% of the 9,980 healthy ones. That's about 100. So of 120 positives, only 20 are sick, 17%. The rule said 99, six times too high. 1% sounds small, but here it's 1% of nearly everyone. Your positive result ruled out everyone who tested negative. What's left is a smaller sample space, these 120 people. Your chance of being sick is the red share of this crowd, 20 out of 20 plus 100. Unrounded, the red count is 20 sick people times 99%. The blue count is 9 healthy people times 1 Divide top and bottom by the 10 we started with 20 people become 2 in 1 and 9 become 998 in 1 The share can't change. These are how common each group is, and these, how often each group tests positive. Bayes' theorem. All it does is shrink the sample space to what the evidence allows, then take the share. Swap the disease for a police watchlist. At the 2017 Champions League final, about 170,000 people were in Cardiff. The watchlists held about 1,200 faces, so even a small error rate per face would swamp the real matches. Face recognition cameras scanned the crowd. They raised 2,400 and 70 alerts. Shrink to the alerts and take the red share. counted 173 as right, 7%. In machine learning, the share of alerts that are right is called precision. The university's evaluators counted 3% here. After a new algorithm and better photos cut the false alarms, they counted 46 at the Six Nations. Back to your test. The title's 99% accuracy is real. But a test that calls Everyone Healthy scores 99.8, more accurate and useless. Your 17% assumes a random screen. Symptoms raise the 1 in 500, and the answer climbs. At 1 in 100, 50%. At 1 in 2, 99, where the rule held. 99% is the test's recall, how often the sick test positive. 17% is its precision, how often the positive are sick.
